newsitem.title: UK: MOF-inspired weakness ebbs, dlr off lows in Europe.
newsitem.headline: MOF-inspired weakness ebbs, dlr off lows in Europe.

text.p: The dollar recovered some composure against the mark and yen in late Europe to end the session down but off lows hit earlier on fears the G3 strong-dollar policy could be set to change, traders and analysts said.
"The dollar selling is running out of steam," said a trader at a European bank.
Analysts noted as mildly supportive U.S. weekly jobless claims at 331,000 against an expected 344,000.
But third-quarter U.S. non-farm productivity which rose 0.2 percent failed to impress the market. "The non-farms figure was smack in line with expectations," said the trader.
At 1557 GMT dollar/mark stood at 1.5087/92, off a session low of 1.5010, against 1.5178/81 in late Europe on Wednesday.
Dollar/yen stood at 111.60/1.70, just off a session low of 111.49, but well down from 113.90/4.00 in late Europe.

The dollar/yen was hit in Europe after Japanese finance minister official Eisuke Sakakibara was quoted as saying dollar/yen's correction of last year plunge was about to end and the Finance Ministry was not trying to weaken the yen further.
"It is clear from his remarks that the Japanese authorities are starting to become concerned about the weakness of the yen," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International.
Analysts said the comments carried special resonance as they came from the man dubbed "Mr Yen" for his part in dragging the yen down from last year's post-war high against the dollar.
But a senior MOF official said late on Thursday that there had been no change in the ministry's stance on currencies.
The Clinton administration, fresh from a landslide election victory on Wednesday, has not made any comments.

But further pressure on the dollar followed commments by the head of the US's National Association of Manufacturers on Thursday that the Clinton administration is likely to de-emphasize the importance of a strong dollar as growth slows.
"As the economy slows, Treasury Secretary (Robert) Rubin will be saying less about the value of a strong dollar," Association President Jerery Jasinowski told reporters.
He said he expected the dollar to "taper off a little bit" as U.S. economic growth slows and long-term interest rates ease.
IBJ's Edmonds said Sakakibara's comments could reflect concerns that Japan's trade surplus has shot up 22.1 percent in the first 20 days of October against a year earlier.
"Japan's trade surplus...in recent months has shown signs of turning around," said Edmonds.
He said there was a risk that if the yen continued to weaken, the newly elected US administration would start to become much more hawkish on trade issues and start to talk the yen up again.

"I think the Japanese authorities have decided to get their retaliation in first...And stabilise the yen around current levels rather than risk a very sharp turnaround in the yen which damages the Japanese recovery," he added.
